title: THE BLAME PIE
goal: Own your real share of a problem without carrying everyone else's.
steps:
1. Imagine A Pie — Imagine a pie that stands for everything that caused the situation.
2. Share The Slices — In your mind, give slices to your choices, other people, circumstances, systems, timing, and chance.
3. Check The Whole — Make sure all slices together equal 100.
4. Find Your Slice — Focus only on your true share.
5. Choose Repair — Picture one repair for your slice. Let the rest stay outside your responsibility.
win: Responsibility shrank to your actual slice, and one repair matched only what belonged to you.
supports:
• Separate guilt from responsibility; name outside factors.
• Make repair smaller than self-punishment; describe the behaviour, not yourself.
• Do not punish yourself for learning; name the mistake.
• Use equal standards; name the exact mistake.
• Avoid global words like always; name the behaviour.
formula_flow: Imagine A Pie → Share The Slices → Check The Whole → Find Your Slice → Choose Repair
safety:
PAUSE
Set it down if sharing turns into punishment or erases genuine accountability.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE LIFE DIRECTION TEST
goal: Choose the next hour by direction, not by the loudest thought.
steps:
1. Picture — Picture two arrows.
2. Make Room — One shows the next hour if you obey the thought; the other reveals what unfolds over sixty minutes when you make room for it but follow a chosen value.
3. Name Likely — Name the likely behaviour at each arrow’s end.
4. Select Direction — Select by direction, not by mental volume.
win: You could see which option moved toward a value even while uncertainty stayed present.
supports:
• Check whose goal; use values to choose trade-offs.
• Make the next hour reflect it; protect important time.
• Act before motivation; choose aligned action.
• Use one priority; do not wait for motivation.
• Review what the action costs; name today's value.
formula_flow: Picture → Make Room → Name Likely → Select Direction
safety:
PAUSE
Choose safety over values exercises during acute crisis or impairment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CLOSE ONE DOOR FOR THIRTY SECONDS
goal: Test each leading option briefly to learn from your reaction without committing.
steps:
1. Close Door — Picture the two leading options. Mentally fade one for thirty seconds and pretend it is unavailable; do not commit.
2. Read Protest — Notice the first specific reaction—relief, disappointment, bargaining, urgency, or no change. Name it in four words or fewer.
3. Reopen Choice — Bring that option back. Repeat once with the other option faded so both reactions receive the same test.
4. Choose Next — Use the clearer reaction as one piece of data, then choose only the next responsible move.
win: Each option was removed and restored once, giving you new data for the next responsible move.
supports:
• Name the non-negotiables; limit the options.
• Reduce the options; ignore imagined regret.
• Use strongest evidence; commit once chosen.
• Stop researching after enough evidence; set a decision deadline.
• Accept one trade-off; choose by the strongest evidence.
formula_flow: Close Door → Read Protest → Reopen Choice → Choose Next
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use pretend closure for urgent, coercive, unsafe, or irreversible choices.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: VALUE BEFORE CERTAINTY
goal: Let a chosen quality guide the next move before certainty arrives.
steps:
1. Ask Quality — Ask, “What quality should the next action carry?” Choose honesty, courage, care, fairness, or patience.
2. Make It Visible — Define one visible movement that expresses that quality today.
3. Let Certainty Wait — Let certainty remain absent while the chosen quality gives direction.
win: One visible action expressed the value you picked even though doubt was still present.
supports:
• Accept the trade-off; make the next hour reflect it.
• Remove one conflicting commitment; name what matters today.
• Keep meaning practical; pick one value for this decision.
• Check whose goal; protect important time.
• Choose aligned action; check whose goal you are chasing.
formula_flow: Ask Quality → Make It Visible → Let Certainty Wait
safety:
PAUSE
Recheck practical facts when uncertainty involves significant legal, financial, or health risk.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE CONTROL GRAVEYARD
goal: Notice which control habits charge more over time than they repay now.
steps:
1. Use Control — Name everything used to control the feeling: checking, avoiding, numbing, arguing, extra certainty, overworking.
2. Picture Short — Beside each, picture the short-term payoff and the six-month bill.

steps:

title: THE THIRD VOICE
goal: Build a response that respects both the feeling and the verified facts.
steps:
1. Open Voices — Complete three lines.
2. Name Feeling — FEELING SAYS: include its full truth.
3. Name Facts — FACTS SAY: include only verified information.
4. Build Wisdom — WISE RESPONSE: honour the need in the first line and the constraints in the second.
5. Use Wisdom — Read only the third line before acting.
win: Your final response included the emotion's need without letting it overwrite reality.
supports:
• Use plain language; check the facts separately.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; let intensity fall.
• Delay the message; check basic needs.
• Name the feeling plainly; slow physical pace.
• Name the emotion; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
formula_flow: Open Voices → Name Feeling → Name Facts → Build Wisdom → Use Wisdom
safety:
PAUSE
Delay major action if either witness is too impaired to give usable information.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

2. Prepare Action — What action is it preparing.

title: CHECK THE BIOLOGICAL VOLUME KNOBS
goal: Check basic body amplifiers before treating the whole reaction as psychological truth.
steps:
1. Review — Review five amplifiers: illness or pain; missed food or hydration; substances or withdrawal; sleep debt; movement deficit or excess.
2. Identify Strongest — Spot the strongest correctable factor.
3. Make Health — Make one health-supporting adjustment before treating the entire reaction as psychological truth.
win: One correctable physical factor was identified and supported before you interpreted the reaction further.
supports:
• Separate feeling from fact; use plain language.
• Check the facts separately; name the emotion.
• Use simple words for the problem; check basic needs.
• Rest before deciding; name the feeling plainly.
• Notice body tension; give the feeling time to move.
formula_flow: Review → Identify Strongest → Make Health
safety:
PAUSE
Seek medical advice for persistent symptoms, medication concerns, or dangerous withdrawal.

title: FEELING OR FIXING?
goal: Decide whether the remaining problem needs soothing, action, or support.
steps:
1. Drop Define — After body alarm drops, define the obstacle without emotional adjectives.
2. Ask Whether — Ask if one specific action could change it.
3. Choose Action — If yes, choose and schedule that action.
4. Return Acceptance — If no, return to acceptance or support.
5. Stop Soothing — Do not keep using soothing when the door requires a key.
win: After the body settled, you could tell whether there was a practical door that needed a key.
supports:
• Avoid symptom searching; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Unclench your jaw; let breaths happen.
• Use ordinary surroundings; let breathing stay natural.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; stop body scanning.
• Reduce caffeine; keep your body supported.

title: FINISH THE LOOK
goal: Let your eyes finish checking the present before deciding where attention belongs.
steps:
1. Let Eyes — Let your eyes move before your head.
2. Scan Left — Slowly scan left, centre, right, behind if safe, and toward an exit.
3. Name Cues — Name present cues of choice, support, and distance from threat.
4. Allow Neck — Allow the neck to follow only within comfort.
5. Place Attention — End by selecting where attention belongs now.
win: Choice, support, distance, and an exit were all visually located without forcing the neck or returning to the past.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; wait before sending messages.
• Use plain language; notice body tension.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; notice what changed physically.
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; slow physical pace.
• Rest before deciding; use simple words for the problem.
formula_flow: Let Eyes → Scan Left → Name Cues → Allow Neck → Place Attention
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid head movement with injury, dizziness, or driving.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ONE DROP, NOT THE OCEAN
goal: Touch only the smallest workable piece of difficult material and recover fully.
steps:
1. Choose Tiniest — Choose the tiniest fragment of the difficult material: one edge, colour, word, or body sensation.
2. Return Fully — Contact it briefly, then return fully to a stabilising cue.
3. Find Dose — Hold the dose that allowed recovery.
4. Use Less — Next practice uses the same or less—not an ambitious leap.
win: A tiny dose was contacted and left without needing a bigger challenge on the next round.
supports:
• Give the surge time to pass; sit somewhere safe.
• Reduce extra stimulation; stop body scanning.
• Keep movements gentle; let breaths happen.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Loosen your shoulders; keep your body supported.
formula_flow: Choose Tiniest → Return Fully → Find Dose → Use Less
safety:
PAUSE
Seek trained support when even minimal contact overwhelms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

ONE DROP, NOT THE OCEAN · SAFETY CLOSER
ritualText:
ONE DROP, NOT THE OCEAN

PLAY TIME
about 1 minute

GOAL
Touch only the smallest workable piece of difficult material and recover fully.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Choose Tiniest — Choose the tiniest fragment of the difficult material: one edge, colour, word, or body sensation.
2. Return Fully — Contact it briefly, then return fully to a stabilising cue.
3. Find Dose — Hold the dose that allowed recovery.
4. Use Less — Next practice uses the same or less—not an ambitious leap.

WIN
A tiny dose was contacted and left without needing a bigger challenge on the next round.

• Give the surge time to pass; sit somewhere safe.
• Reduce extra stimulation; stop body scanning.
• Keep movements gentle; let breaths happen.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Loosen your shoulders; keep your body supported.

MIND BEND
The useful dose is the one your system can digest — more intensity is not automatically more learning.

FORMULA FLOW
Choose Tiniest → Return Fully → Find Dose → Use Less

SAFETY
PAUSE
Seek trained support when even minimal contact overwhelms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MAP THE EARLY STEADINESS SIGNALS
goal: Notice early loss of steadiness and know exactly when self-help should stop.
steps:
1. Name Early Change — Name one early sign that present-time steadiness is weakening.
2. Choose External Grounding — Choose an eyes-open external grounding action that usually remains safe.
3. Set Stop Threshold — Set the point where all self-help must stop.
4. Pick Support Route — Choose the support route you will use and make it easy to find.
5. Share The Plan — Share the short plan with someone trustworthy before it is needed.
win: You had a grounding action, a stop point, and a support route ready before the alarm became stronger.
supports:
• Contact someone trusted; stop if you feel less present.
• Contact someone you trust; orient to today's date and place.
• Hold something familiar; choose gentle, ordinary movement.
• Keep your eyes open if safer; name today's date.
• Keep lighting comfortable; use familiar surroundings.
formula_flow: Name Early Change → Choose External Grounding → Set Stop Threshold → Pick Support Route → Share The Plan
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open. Use only present-day room, date, place and support orientation. Do not revisit memories in detail, use trauma imagery, intensify sensations, or attempt unsupervised processing. Stop for flooding, dissociation, or weakened orientation and connect with qualified human support.
This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

title: LET BREATH BREATHE YOU
goal: Let breathing happen by itself while you simply notice its movement.
steps:
1. Follow Breaths — Follow three natural breaths exactly as they occur.
2. Leave Breath Alone — Do not deepen, slow, count, or improve them.
3. Start — Notice where each begins by itself and where it ends without instruction.
4. Let Body — Between breaths, let the body choose again.
5. Witness Motion — Your only action is witnessing what already knows how to move.
win: Three breaths began and ended without being corrected, deepened, slowed, or counted.
supports:
• Reduce commentary; return to the room.
• Use fewer words; notice where attention goes.
• Drop the need to solve it; notice the thought.
• Do not debate every detail; avoid building a larger story.
• Use simple present-tense facts; notice the thought, then step back.
formula_flow: Follow Breaths → Leave Breath Alone → Start → Let Body → Witness Motion
safety:
PAUSE
Use outward sensory contact if breath attention increases panic or air hunger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RHYTHM BEFORE DEPTH
goal: Settle into an easy breathing rhythm before changing depth or volume.
steps:
1. Choose Slow — Choose a comfortable pace where inhale and exhale stay easy.
2. Count Rhythm — Count four gentle cycles without forcing depth or lung volume.
3. Continue Easy — Keep the same comfortable rhythm for four more cycles.
4. Release Count — Drop the counting and allow one natural breath.
win: Eight comfortable cycles stayed steady, then counting dropped away into one natural breath.
supports:
• Sip water if it helps; reduce caffeine.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; let breathing stay natural.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Wait out the surge; keep your body supported.

title: WHAT SURVIVES THREE STATES?
goal: Test which identity claims still make sense across waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
steps:
1. Picture Appears — Picture what appears in waking, what appears in dreams, and what is absent or inferred in deep sleep.
2. Ask Claims — Ask which claims of identity remain supported across all three.
3. Hold Conclusions — Hold conclusions lightly; this is an inquiry into ongoing sense, not a demand for belief.
win: The inquiry held several states in view without forcing a final belief about what you are.
supports:
• Do one action for your life; choose your own measure.
• Use your own timeline; notice what you cannot see.
• Compare with your past self; name one thing already working.
• Stop checking their numbers; check your own progress.
• Use your own priorities; limit social media exposure.
formula_flow: Picture Appears → Ask Claims → Hold Conclusions
safety:
PAUSE
Discontinue if sleep-related inquiry worsens insomnia or unreality.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SAME VALUE, TWO OUTCOMES
goal: Keep the same value steady across both success and failure.
steps:
1. Imagine Action — Imagine the action succeeding.
2. State Governing — State what that value asks of you next.
3. Imagine Failing — Imagine it failing.
4. State Value — State how the same value responds there.
5. Let Outcome — Let outcome alter strategy, not your ethical centre.
win: The imagined outcome changed strategy, but the value still supplied a next action in either direction.
supports:
• Notice absolute words like always; test the assumption.
• Ask what would change your mind; separate possibility from probability.
• Check the base rate; look for one missing fact.
• Check what you actually know; question absolute words.
• Delay the verdict; ask what else could fit.

safety:
PAUSE

title: EMPTY THE MENTAL COUNTERTOP
goal: Empty every loose obligation into one trusted place before deciding what comes first.
steps:
1. Question Promise — Catch every task, question, promise, and loose obligation into one trusted place.
2. Empty First — Do not organise while emptying.
3. Sort Entries — When the mind offers silence, sort entries into do, schedule, delegate, reference, or delete.
4. Choose Physical — Choose only the first physical action.
win: The mental pile reached silence, then each item received a home and only one physical action remained active.
supports:
• Keep one task visible; use one screen.
• Take a short break; park secondary tasks.
• Clear visual clutter; finish or park one open loop.
• Return after interruptions; put the phone out of reach.
• Return to one target; close what you do not need.

title: THE REQUEST SPINE
goal: State the situation, its impact, your exact request, and why cooperation helps.
steps:
1. Describe Situation — Say the visible situation.
2. Express Impact — Express its impact.
3. Assert Request — Assert the exact request or no.
4. Reinforce Cooperation — Reinforce why cooperation helps.
5. Picture Sentence — Picture one sentence for each part, then deliver the leanest version.
win: The message reached its request without detouring into accusation, vagueness, or excess explanation.
supports:
• Repeat the same wording calmly; decide your limit before answering.
• Keep consequences realistic; take time before saying yes.
• State consequences clearly; let guilt pass.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; notice resentment as a warning.
• Repeat without arguing; leave their reaction with them.

title: IMPACT IS KNOWN; MOTIVE IS PENDING
goal: Respond to behaviour and impact while leaving the other person's motive undecided.
steps:
1. Separate Unknown — Picture three separate statements: their behaviour; what effect it had; what you do not know about intention.
2. Base — Base your next boundary on behaviour and impact.
3. Leave Motive — Leave motive open until reliable evidence or direct communication updates it.
win: A boundary became possible without needing to prove why the other person did what they did.
supports:
• Notice when checking stops helping; choose a good-enough option.
• Use a decision deadline; ask what is controllable now.
• Set a limit on checking; name what is unknown.
• Accept small risk; act on the safest workable option.
• Delay reassurance seeking; accept a small margin of risk.

title: BRAID THE SIGNALS
goal: Let two competing signals share attention before deciding which one matters.
steps:
1. Choose Signals — Choose the two signals fighting for attention.
2. Alternate B — Alternate A–B–A–B at a slow fixed rhythm.
3. Hold Time — Then hold both at the same time for one interval, noticing difference without choosing.
4. Decide After — Decide only after the braid is complete.
win: A–B alternation became simultaneous awareness, and the decision waited until both signals had been fully represented.
supports:
• Use one screen; keep one task visible.
• Reduce nearby noise; finish or park one open loop.
• Use one window at a time; mute alerts.
• Clear visual clutter; silence nonessential notifications.
• Choose one target; take a real screen break.
formula_flow: Choose Signals → Alternate B → Hold Time → Decide After
safety:
PAUSE
Do not braid a safety alarm with pressure to ignore it.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MATCH THE PRESSURE, THEN ZERO IT
goal: Match two sides of physical pressure, then lower both together back to zero.
steps:
1. Press Equal — Press palms together—or both hands into one cushion—at about twenty percent effort. Keep breathing ordinary.
2. Match Force — Adjust until neither side wins and the pressure feels equal. Hold that match for two seconds.
3. Step Down — Lower both sides together through three gentle levels: fifteen, ten, then five percent.
4. Reach Zero — Reach zero, rest both hands on a stable surface, and observe whether the urge to press returns.
win: Equal resistance stepped down through lighter levels until your hands rested and the urge to press could be checked.
supports:
• Keep your hands busy; drink some water.
• Remember urges peak and fall; avoid bargaining with the urge.
• Ride the peak; use your hands.
• Make access less convenient; move away from the cue.
• Delay acting for ten minutes; make access harder.
formula_flow: Press Equal → Match Force → Step Down → Reach Zero
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid this with pain, hand or joint injury, numbness, breath holding, or any unsafe physical symptom.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: COUNT EVERY OPEN LOOP
goal: Count every unresolved mental loop without trying to solve any of them yet.
steps:
1. Question Task — Name every unresolved promise, question, task, decision, and waiting item without solving any.
2. Use Line — Use one line each.
3. Imagine Boundary — When nothing else appears for thirty seconds, imagine a boundary around the inventory and choose a separate processing time.
win: Promises, tasks, questions, decisions, and waiting items became a bounded inventory with a later processing time.
supports:
• Close what you do not need; silence nonessential notifications.
• Keep one task visible; park secondary tasks.
• Close extra tabs; use a short focus block.
• Mute alerts; return after interruptions.
• Protect one focus block; choose one target.
formula_flow: Question Task → Use Line → Imagine Boundary
safety:
PAUSE
End the capture if list-making increases overwhelm without containment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WANT NOW / PROTECT LATER
goal: Acknowledge what the urge wants now while protecting what future life still needs.
steps:
1. Picture Urge — Picture what the present urge wants, then what future life is worth protecting.
2. Name Cost — Name the cost each imposes on the other.
3. Choose Action — Choose one action that acknowledges desire while keeping the valued asset intact.
win: The chosen move made room for desire without sacrificing the longer-term asset you named.
supports:
• Leave the trigger; remember urges peak and fall.
• Ride the peak; change rooms if possible.
• Keep your hands busy; eat or drink if hunger matters.
• Drink some water; use your hands.
• Delay ten minutes; make access harder.
formula_flow: Picture Urge → Name Cost → Choose Action
safety:
PAUSE
Seek support when cravings threaten safety, sobriety, or financial control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PREVIEW THE AFTER
goal: Picture the ten seconds after completion clearly enough to make the first move easier.
steps:
1. Protect Enjoyed — Picture a ten-second scene immediately after completion: what is lighter, available, learned, protected, or enjoyed.
2. Include Sensory — Include a sensory marker plus one practical consequence.
3. State Accessible — Begin the task while that specific after-state remains accessible.
win: A sensory after-scene and one practical benefit stayed available while the task began.
supports:
• Name today's date; notice room temperature.
• Feel your feet; reduce sensory input if needed.
• Notice where your body is supported; hear one real sound.
• Feel the chair; notice temperature and texture.
• Notice three colours; keep your eyes on something steady.
formula_flow: Protect Enjoyed → Include Sensory → State Accessible
safety:

title: THE BORING DOSE
goal: Practise a small, fixed dose of boredom without adding stimulation or extending the challenge.
steps:
1. Choose Boring — Choose a safe boring task and decide on ten slow breaths.
2. Remove Extras Mentally — Decide that no extra stimulation will be added during those breaths.
3. Stay — Notice boredom’s body sensations until the tenth breath.
4. End Cleanly — Stop there, even if you could continue; increase future doses slowly.
win: Ten slow breaths passed with the boring task unchanged, and the exercise stopped exactly at the planned dose.
supports:
• Use ordinary surroundings; unclench your jaw and shoulders.
• Wait out the surge; keep movements gentle.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; reduce caffeine.
• Let breathing stay natural; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Reduce extra stimulation; loosen your shoulders.
formula_flow: Choose Boring → Remove Extras Mentally → Stay → End Cleanly
safety:
PAUSE
Adapt for attention disorders and never use boredom as punishment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT PREPARATION DID WORRY ACTUALLY PRODUCE?
goal: Separate the preparation worry produced from the simulation it keeps repeating.
steps:
1. Create Worry — Name every concrete preparation created by the worry.
2. Separate Useful — Separate useful actions from repeated simulation.
3. Prepare Name — If what you named contains a real gap, prepare once.
4. Remain Name — If no gap remains, label further worry UNPAID OVERTIME.
win: Any real gap was prepared once; when no gap remained, further worry lost its claim to useful work.
supports:
• Begin with the easiest part; start with one minute.
• Set a two-minute timer; skip extra setup.
• Open the task; remove one barrier.
• Prepare the task in advance; use a visible cue.
• Lower standards briefly; start physically.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not dismiss new information simply because worry has repeated.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MARK THE QUALITY DROP
goal: Stop when your thinking quality shows clear signs of decline and keep the last reliable conclusion.
steps:
1. Repeat No — Define your personal decline signs in advance: rereading, harsher certainty, slower comprehension, repeated searches, no new distinctions.
2. Stop Last — When two appear, stop and hold the last reliable conclusion.
3. Start Recovery — Recovery precedes any reopening.
win: Two personal warning signs triggered closure before more searching could degrade comprehension further.
supports:
• Check what you actually know; add the missing context.
• Use a real example; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Separate guess from evidence; ask what else could fit.
• Look for one missing fact; question absolute words.
• Delay the verdict; separate possibility from probability.
formula_flow: Repeat No → Stop Last → Start Recovery
safety:
PAUSE
Continue only when delay creates greater risk than reduced quality.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE TURNING POINT AT HALF SPEED
goal: Replay only the turning point slowly enough to keep observation separate from motive.
steps:
1. Recall Exchange — Choose no more than ten seconds of the interaction, beginning before the moment that felt different.
2. Halve Speed — Run those ten seconds once in imagination at half speed. Keep only what you can actually observe: words, pauses, volume, face, and movement.
3. Shift — Stop at the first change and name it without motive: ‘the pause lengthened,’ ‘the volume rose,’ or ‘the reply shortened.’
4. Keep Fact — Keep that one fact. End the review before building another explanation.
win: One visible change—pause, volume, face, movement, or reply length—was kept while the review ended before explanation multiplied.
supports:
• Start physically; lower the quality bar.
• Use a visible cue; enter through easy work.
• Lower standards briefly; touch the first item.
• Choose tiny action; make it visible.
• Start before you feel ready; stop planning after one action.
formula_flow: Recall Exchange → Halve Speed → Shift → Keep Fact
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if this review raises distress, becomes compulsive, or concerns abuse or danger that requires support and protection.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: AUCTION THE NEXT ATTENTION BLOCK
goal: Make active concerns compete for one attention block using consequence and reversibility, not noise.
steps:
1. Let Active — Let each active concern bid on urgency, consequence, reversibility, and information value.
2. Total — Total the four ratings.
3. Protect Block — Award one protected block to the highest bidder and deny all others entry until time expires.
4. Update Evidence — Re-auction with updated evidence.
win: Urgency, consequence, reversibility, and information value awarded the next block to one concern while the others waited.
supports:
• Choose by the strongest evidence; ignore imagined regret.
• Commit once chosen; name must-haves.
• Ask what failure would cost; reduce the options.
• Set a deadline; choose the option you can support.
• Accept one trade-off; stop researching after enough evidence.
formula_flow: Let Active → Total → Protect Block → Update Evidence
safety:
PAUSE
Emergency signals may override the auction immediately.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TURN THE LOOP INTO FIVE ICONS
goal: Turn a repetitive thought loop into simple images and interrupt the first repeated meaning.
steps:
1. No Sentences — Imagine five boxes. Do not use full sentences.
2. Imagine Five Signs — Give each of the last five thought turns one simple inner picture.
3. Spot The Return — Notice the first picture whose meaning comes back later.
4. Choose An Exit — At the next box, picture one real fact to check or one small action to take, then stop imagining.
win: The first returning icon exposed the loop, then one real fact or action replaced another thought turn.
supports:
• Name one useful action; use your hands.
• Stop solving the unsolvable; do something that needs your hands.
• Shift attention outward; set a clear stopping point.
• Ask if any new information exists; name one action.
• Limit how long you review it; end the replay.
formula_flow: No Sentences → Imagine Five Signs → Spot The Return → Choose An Exit
safety:
PAUSE
Do not imagine this while driving; stop if the mental sequence becomes compulsive, perfectionistic, or more distressing than the thought.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: REMEMBER THE FUTURE IN ADVANCE
goal: Imagine the scene just after completion, then trace backward to the first movement you can do now.
steps:
1. Create Memory — Create a memory-like scene set just after completing the action.
2. Include Time — Include time, location, body posture, one sensory cue, along with what you did when difficulty appeared.
3. Look Backward — Look backward from that imagined completion to the first real movement and do it now.
win: A future memory supplied posture, sensory detail, and a coping response that led directly back to a real first action.
supports:
• Feel your feet; return to one real sound.
• Slow your physical pace; keep eyes open.
• Keep your eyes on something steady; hear one real sound.
• Notice three colours; look around the room.
• Notice room temperature; feel both feet.
formula_flow: Create Memory → Include Time → Look Backward
safety:
PAUSE
Keep future scenes realistic rather than using fantasy as avoidance.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: INTERVIEW THE OBSTACLE
goal: Ask the obstacle what it is protecting and negotiate one step that respects the valid need.
steps:
1. Give Obstacle — Give the obstacle a character and ask three questions: What are you protecting.
2. Ask Fear — What do you fear will happen.
3. Make Step — What would make one step acceptable.
4. Picture Negotiate — Picture its answers, then negotiate a small action that protects the valid need without handing over total control.
win: Fear, protection, and conditions for movement became explicit enough to make a small agreement possible.
supports:
• Start smaller; make it visible.
• Do the easiest useful part; set a two-minute timer.
• Choose tiny action; prepare first.
• Open only what you need; start with one minute.
• Touch the first item; open the task.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not personify intrusive voices or experiences if that worsens symptoms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: IMAGINE THE INNER MACHINE
goal: Map the full trigger-to-result loop and change one link instead of fighting the whole system.
steps:
1. Imagine The Parts — Imagine the trigger, meaning, physical feeling, urge, action, result, and feedback.
2. See The Links — Imagine how each part affects the next and where the loop returns.
3. Find the Lever — Notice one place where a small change may shift the whole loop.
4. Test It — Try that small change once.
win: A single point in the sequence shifted once, creating fresh evidence about how the larger pattern responds.
supports:
• Eat if hungry; move away from the cue.
• Avoid bargaining with the urge; tell someone early.
• Make access less convenient; drink some water.
• Eat or drink if hunger matters; delay ten minutes.
• Do one incompatible activity; keep your hands busy.
formula_flow: Imagine The Parts → See The Links → Find the Lever → Test It
safety:
PAUSE
Keep the mental picture simple. Stop if you begin analysing without taking action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BUILD THE MINIATURE FIRST
goal: Test a low-risk miniature of the idea before paying the full cost of the real version.
steps:

title: WHAT WOULD THIS FACT CHANGE?
goal: Collect only facts that could actually change what you decide.
steps:
1. Point Positive — For every desired data point, picture how a positive, negative, or neutral result would alter the decision.
2. Stop Collecting — If no result changes action, stop collecting it.
3. Test Relevance — Prioritise the fact with the largest possible decision swing.
win: A desired data point stayed only if at least one possible result would change your action.
supports:
• Use a visible cue; start before you feel ready.
• Use two minutes; touch the first item.
• Open only what you need; enter through easy work.
• Remove one barrier; choose tiny action.
• Remove one obvious distraction; cut the task.

safety:
PAUSE
Keep legally, clinically, or ethically required information even when choice impact seems small.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE PAST INVESTMENT GETS NO NEW VOTE
goal: Ignore what is already spent and compare the choices only from today forward.
steps:
1. Hide Already — Hide what has already been spent.
2. Compare Options — Compare options from today forward using remaining cost, likely benefit, opportunity cost, and risk.
3. Remove Sunk Vote — Reveal the past investment afterward only for learning, never for sharing.

• Delay the verdict; check another angle.
• Ask what else could fit; test the assumption.
• Check the whole situation; notice absolute words like always.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check the base rate.

title: PROTECT THE VALID CHOICE

steps:

title: BREAK THE EXPECTED SEQUENCE
goal: Test one respectful alternative to an expected life sequence without attacking the whole culture around it.
steps:
1. Picture Culturally — Picture the culturally expected next step.
2. Name Benefits — Name who benefits, what value it serves, and what it costs you.
3. Generate — Generate one respectful alternative sequence.
4. Test Small — Test a small part without declaring war on the whole culture.
win: Who benefits, what the norm serves, and what it costs you became visible before one small alternative was tried.
supports:
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; question absolute words.
• Test the assumption; delay the verdict.
• Use a real example; check the whole situation.
• Check what you actually know; separate guess from evidence.
• Check another angle; use recent, concrete evidence.

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: HIDE THE CROWD’S ANSWER
goal: Form your own quality judgment before looking at ratings, likes, rankings, or social consensus.
steps:
1. Group Preference — Before seeing ratings, likes, rankings, or group preference, assess quality using your own criteria.
2. Hold Judgement — Hold the judgement and reasons.
3. View Crowd — Reveal social proof afterward and change your view only if the crowd supplies new evidence, not mere numbers.
win: Your criteria and reasons existed before social proof appeared, so numbers could add evidence without replacing judgment.
supports:
• Separate possibility from probability; use a real example.
• Notice absolute words like always; use current facts.
• Check the whole situation; use recent, concrete evidence.
• Question absolute words; ask what else could fit.
• Ask what would disprove it; delay major conclusions when upset.
formula_flow: Group Preference → Hold Judgement → View Crowd
safety:
PAUSE
Use expert consensus appropriately where specialised knowledge matters.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: GIVE THE BELIEF A POSTCODE
goal: Shrink a broad belief until it states where, when, and with whom it actually fits.
steps:
1. Name The Belief — Say the belief silently.
2. Imagine Four Limits — Think about when, where, with whom, and under what conditions it may be true.
3. Test Inside — Picture one real case where it fits.
4. Test Outside — Picture one real case where the belief does not fit.
5. Shrink the Rule — Say a smaller, more accurate version of the belief.
win: One fitting case and one exception produced a smaller statement that was more accurate than the original rule.
supports:
• Repeat without arguing; keep the limit simple.
• Take time before saying yes; repeat the same wording calmly.
• Use a short no; keep consequences realistic.
• State consequences clearly; delay your answer.
• Offer only genuine options; use one clear sentence.
formula_flow: Name The Belief → Imagine Four Limits → Test Inside → Test Outside → Shrink the Rule
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use belief boundaries to minimise abuse, discrimination, medical facts, legal duties, or immediate danger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TWO-SECOND LAUNCH
goal: Use one opening line to trigger the first action and save a return point.
steps:
1. Show Target — Say one usable opening line.
2. Take Action — Complete the first action.
3. Set Return — Settle on the restart marker you can return to.
win: The first move happened, and a specific marker showed where the next session could continue.
supports:
• Enter through easy work; start with one minute.
• Start smaller; stop planning after one action.
• Start before you feel ready; begin while unsure.
• Start physically; prepare the task in advance.
• Cut the task; touch the first item.
formula_flow: Show Target → Take Action → Set Return
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if this makes you less steady, more distressed, or less able to act safely. Use human, professional, medical, or emergency support when the situation needs more than self-help.
This brief reset is not diagnosis, treatment, or emergency care.

title: RESTART MARK
goal: Cut the scope to one result, remove unrelated input, and leave a fresh return point.
steps:
1. Show Target — Name a fresh opening line.
2. Cut Scope — Reduce the scope to one result.
3. Quiet Cues — Remove unrelated distractions.
4. Set Bookmark — Place the restart point.
win: One workable outcome replaced the larger job and the next entry point stayed obvious.
supports:
• Restart quickly; lower the first demand.
• Choose a rough beginning; start smaller.
• Start physically; do the easiest useful part.
• Use one window; lower standards briefly.
• Shrink the first action; start with one minute.

ritualText:
ONE CUE LANDING

PLAY TIME
60–120 seconds

GOAL
Face the task, say the first sentence, and let the prepared answer start at normal speed.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Set Stance — Face your body toward the task.
2. Practice Line — Say only the first sentence, then stop.
3. Speak Once — Say the prepared first answer at a normal pace.
4. Delay Score — Name the review you will postpone until after delivery.

WIN
The opening landed without being expanded by pre-performance analysis, and review stayed postponed.

• Ask to repeat; look up regularly.
• Use one friendly face; finish one sentence at a time.
• Say what you know first; do not apologise.
• Finish one sentence; plant both feet.
• Use a short pause; look at one friendly face.

MIND BEND
The first sentence can function as a landing cue. Once speech begins, retrieval often has something to attach to.

FORMULA FLOW
Set Stance → Practice Line → Speak Once → Delay Score

SAFETY
PAUSE
Stop if this makes you less steady, more distressed, or less able to act safely. Use human, professional, medical, or emergency support when the situation needs more than self-help.
This brief reset is not diagnosis, treatment, or emergency care.

goal: Compare the loudest outside opinion with one fact from your own situation before choosing.
steps:
1. Fit Load — Notice the strongest outside opinion.

win: The next decision survived contact with your own evidence and still felt authored by you.
supports:

• Limit social media exposure; choose your own measure.
• Track progress by your values; avoid one-person benchmarks.
• Notice what you cannot see; name one thing already working.
• Do one action for your life; use your own priorities.

title: THE ROOM COMES BACK
goal: Re-establish the room, your body, and human contact when things feel unreal.
steps:
1. Look Around — Mark your current physical location.
2. Name Signal — Name the present body signal.
3. Ease Speed — Slow your hand speed one notch.
4. Move Once — Name the cue, then take a step away from it.
5. Call Support — Tell the chosen support person what you need.
win: You named where you were, slowed one movement, stepped away from a cue, and told someone what support you needed.
supports:
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; give the surge time to pass.
• Sit somewhere safe; let breathing stay natural.
• Loosen your shoulders; reduce extra stimulation.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; keep your body supported.
• Keep movements gentle; sip water if it helps.
formula_flow: Look Around → Name Signal → Ease Speed → Move Once → Call Support
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open and orient to the room. Stop if symptoms intensify, you feel faint, or a medical problem may be possible. Call Triple Zero (000) for an emergency; otherwise use qualified medical advice. Do not induce or test symptoms.
This is brief self-help, not diagnosis or treatment.

title: THE INSULT ANCHOR
goal: Keep a status threat from becoming retaliation while preserving the factual boundary.
steps:
1. Delay Action — Do not send, confront, drive toward, or act on the first retaliatory urge.
2. Slow Pace — Slow your pace and let one full exhale finish naturally.
3. State Boundary — Say the boundary in one factual sentence without threat, diagnosis, or character attack.
4. Hold Send — If you cannot say it safely and briefly, do not send or deliver it yet.
win: No irreversible action was taken and the boundary could be stated without threat, diagnosis, or character attack.
supports:
• Delay the message; stick to current facts.
• Name the issue; drop old grievances.
• Lower your voice; avoid empty threats.
• Use one clear request; leave the argument.
• Keep consequences proportionate; return when calmer.
formula_flow: Delay Action → Slow Pace → State Boundary → Hold Send
safety:
PAUSE
Do not send, drive, confront, threaten, or act while control feels reduced. Move away from weapons and hazards; use human or emergency support if anyone may be unsafe.

title: DO NOT ACT ON THE SUSPICION ALONE
play_time: ACT NOW — MOVE TO LIVE SUPPORT
goal: Do not act on an unverified suspicion; stay with a reliable person while it is professionally assessed.
steps:
1. Freeze Risky Action — Do not confront, travel, spend, post, or retaliate on the suspicion.
2. Contact Trusted Person — Call someone known for being calm and reliable.
3. Share Exact Concern — State what you noticed and what you fear without adding certainty.
4. Accept Outside Check — Let that person contact urgent professional help with you.
5. Stay Connected — Remain together until the concern is safely assessed.
win: Confrontation and other irreversible actions stayed paused while a trusted person helped connect you with urgent support.
supports:
• Stay close to trusted people.
• Delay important decisions.
• Keep the environment calm and familiar.
• Share what feels hard to verify.
• Ask for professional support today.
formula_flow: Freeze Risky Action → Contact Trusted Person → Share Exact Concern → Accept Outside Check → Stay Connected
safety:
PAUSE
IMMEDIATE DANGER OR POSSIBLE MEDICAL EMERGENCY: call Triple Zero (000) now.
24/7 CRISIS SUPPORT: call Lifeline 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14.
Stay with a safe person and follow qualified support. Do not return to ordinary rituals.

title: REASSURANCE ENDS HERE
goal: Stop outsourcing certainty to reassurance and decide from the evidence you actually have.
steps:
1. Hold Question — Name the evidence that is actually missing.
2. Sample It — Say the idea in one real-world sentence.
3. Review Once — Review the fact once, choose the next move, and stop.
win: The missing evidence was named, the fact was reviewed once, and the next move happened without another reassurance round.
supports:

• Stop reopening choices; choose a good-enough option.
• Leave one doubt; notice when checking stops helping.
• Accept a small margin of risk; limit checking.
• Set a limit on checking; delay reassurance.

title: THE NO-CHECK DECISION
goal: Make the needed decision through one chosen lens and stop checking whether the intrusive idea has disappeared.
steps:
1. Name Decision — Name the decision you actually need to make.
2. Pick Lens — Pick one lens that counts for this round—safe, useful, kind, necessary, or time-bound.
3. Choose Fit — Choose the option that best fits that lens.
4. Close Choice — Say, “Decision made for now.”
5. Skip Check — Continue for one minute without checking whether the idea is gone.
win: One criterion guided the choice, the decision was closed for now, and the next minute continued without intrusion monitoring.
supports:
• Return to the task; notice mental content.
• Delay reassurance; reduce deliberate monitoring.
• Do not neutralise; return to the current task.
• Avoid confessing for relief; allow uncertainty.
• Let thoughts pass; skip confession for relief.
